title: Detection of Hardware
summary: This strategy detects hardware fingerprinting against your environment, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1592.001 (Gather Victim Host Information: Hardware). Before choosing an exploit, an adversary wants to know which devices you run and what they are: router and firewall models, virtualisation platform, industrial control equipment, and the small set of details that a port scan or a malformed request reveals. The technique happens at the network edge, outside endpoint telemetry, so detection leans on firewall and intrusion detection records, web server and reverse proxy logs, honeypot deployments, and external scans of your own address space. What makes it detectable is repetition and breadth: a single failed connection is background noise, while a sequence of probes that walks through a device inventory in minutes follows the shape of reconnaissance. The hardest part is separating research, vulnerability scanning by third parties, and ordinary internet noise from deliberate, targeted pre attack collection.

beginner.definition: Hardware fingerprinting means finding out which physical devices a company runs and how they are built. Attackers do this before they attack, so they can pick the right tool. This detection looks for repeated probing of your network from outside, especially probing that checks many ports or device types.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every device answers questions, even when it says no. A reply can reveal a brand, a model, or an old version with a known weakness. Attackers compare those answers with public lists of vulnerable equipment. If you never watch this probing, you learn about the interest only when the attack starts. Early warning gives your team time to patch or to hide the device from the internet.
howItWorks: Your firewall and intrusion detection system record connections, including refused and blocked ones.
The detection groups those records by the outside source address and the time window.
It looks for one source touching many ports or many devices in a short period.
Enrichment adds context, such as whether the source is a known scanner or a rented server.
The scoring step highlights sources that scanned specific device types, such as remote management ports.
The analyst reviews the pattern, blocks clear abuse, and confirms that the targeted devices are patched and hidden.
beginner.example: Picture a night watchman walking past a row of houses. A single person trying one door handle is normal. But the same person walking down the street, trying every door, then stopping to look closely at the windows and the alarm boxes, is planning something. The walking pattern, not the single door, tells the story.
takeaways: Probing usually comes from the internet, so network and server logs are the main evidence.
One failed connection means little. Many probes from one source in a short time means a lot.
The real fix is removing unnecessary exposure, not only blocking the source addresses.

objectives: Explain how hardware details exposed at the network edge help an adversary select an exploit
Identify the perimeter telemetry that records probing of your devices and services
Build a detection that scores scan breadth and device specific probing by source
Separate routine internet noise and authorised scanning from targeted reconnaissance
Recommend exposure reduction steps such as removing management interfaces from the internet
dataSources: Firewall logs of blocked inbound connection attempts including source address, destination port, and rule name
Intrusion detection or prevention alerts for port scan and service probe signatures with source and destination
Web server or reverse proxy access logs showing requests that identify device models or request unusual paths
Honeypot or canary service logs recording interactions with decoy management interfaces
External attack surface scan results for your public address ranges including exposed service banners
logic: The detection looks for a concentrated burst of connection attempts from one external source toward many addresses or many ports in your public ranges, especially attempts that target remote management, virtualisation, or industrial device interfaces rather than common web ports alone. The fields that must be correlated are the source address and its autonomous system, the destination address and port, the rule or signature that fired, the request path or banner where available, and the timestamps that define the burst. The benign version is a scheduled vulnerability scan from a known provider, a monitoring service checking a single port, or the ordinary background noise of the internet hitting an exposed service repeatedly from many unrelated addresses. The malicious version is a single source showing breadth, moving from discovery to device specific probing, and often resolving a name first so that the destination set looks deliberate rather than random.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Breadth First Probing of Device Ports From a Single External Source
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   category: firewall
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event.action: deny
#     destination.port|in: [22, 23, 80, 161, 443, 3389, 5900, 8080, 8443, 44818, 502]
#   filter_known_scanners:
#     source.ip|in: approved_scanner_ranges
#   condition: selection and not filter_known_scanners | count() by source.ip > 40 within 10m
# level: medium
falsePositives: Approved third party vulnerability scanning and penetration testing performed on a schedule from known ranges
Internet wide research scanning projects that probe every public address without targeting your organisation
Uptime and availability monitoring services that check a small set of public ports every minute
Shodan style indexing or certificate search crawlers that revisit your address space after a new certificate is issued
Misconfigured backup or inventory tools on a partner network that repeatedly retry connections to decommissioned addresses
tuningNotes: Allowlist the address ranges of your approved scanning providers and your own external testing hosts, and verify those entries every quarter because testing contracts change. Require a breadth threshold such as forty distinct destination ports or twenty distinct addresses within a ten minute window, and ignore single port repeats, which are almost always noise. Restrict the rule to address ranges that host devices with management interfaces rather than your whole public space, and baseline the normal deny volume per range so your threshold fits the environment. The coverage you lose by raising the threshold is slow, patient reconnaissance that spreads its probes over days, so keep a long window report that counts distinct probes per source per month as a hunting query.
